items.prompt: What does git push --force do to the remote branch?
choices: It moves the branch pointer to your tip, skipping the safety check
It merges your commits with the remote's commits
It deletes the repository and re-creates it
items.explanation: Force-push replaces where the branch points; it never merges.

items.prompt: A branch on the remote is best described as:
choices: A folder holding a copy of the files
A named pointer to one commit
A list of every teammate's changes
items.explanation: A branch is just a label attached to a tip commit.

items.prompt: After a force-push moves the pointer, commits only reachable from the old tip are:
choices: Automatically merged into the new tip
Copied to a backup branch by the server
No longer reachable from that branch
items.explanation: Nothing points to them from the branch any more.

items.prompt: Does a force-push reconcile your history with the remote's?
choices: No, it replaces the remote's position with yours
Yes, line by line like a merge
Yes, but only for commits from the same author
items.explanation: There is no reconciliation step; the pointer is simply overwritten.

items.prompt: Which push skips the check that remote commits are not lost?
choices: git push
git push --force
git fetch
items.explanation: Plain push enforces the check; force turns it off.

items.prompt: Force-pushing to a branch only you ever push to is:
choices: Always destructive to your own history
Impossible without admin rights
Usually harmless, since no one else's commits are at stake
items.explanation: The danger comes from other people's commits, so a private branch is low risk.

items.prompt: A commit is reachable from a tip when:
choices: You can walk backward through parent links from the tip and arrive at it
It was made today by the same author
It has a tag attached
items.explanation: Reachability is about following parents from the tip.

items.prompt: After a force-push, the dropped commit is best described as:
choices: Erased from every clone instantly
Still stored for a while, but no branch leads to it
Turned into a merge commit
items.explanation: Objects stay until garbage collection; the branch just stops pointing to them.

items.prompt: The remote branch is A-B-C-D (tip D). You force-push your local A-B-C-E (tip E). Where does the branch point, and is D still reachable from it?
choices: It points at D, and E is added after it
It points at E, and D is not reachable
It points at E, and D stays reachable through C
It points at C, the last commit both share
items.explanation: The pointer moves to E. D hangs off the old tip only, so walking back from E never reaches it.
items.reference:
What force-push moves
📌 branch = pointer to one tip commit
➡️ force-push: pointer jumps to your tip
🕳️ commits only on the old side lose their branch
Why: the loss is reachability, not a merge or an instant delete.
items.learnMore:
Force-push is a pointer move

Nothing is combined or compared. The old tip stops being part of the branch's history, and anyone who only looks at the branch no longer sees those commits.

Common mistake

Thinking the other person's commit was deleted from disk. It is still stored somewhere for a while, just unreachable from the branch.
items.reflection: Think of a shared playlist that anyone can replace with their own saved version. What would you want to check first before replacing it?

items.prompt: Which statement about force-push is accurate?
choices: It deletes unreachable commit objects the moment it runs
It creates a merge commit that preserves both lines
It moves the pointer; unreachable commits are cleaned up only later by garbage collection
It only rewrites commits authored by the person pushing
items.explanation: Force-push changes a reference, not object storage, so the loss is of reachability rather than instant deletion.

items.prompt: The remote is A-B-C. You force-push A-B-C-D, which is strictly ahead. What is lost?
choices: Commit C, because the pointer moved
Commit B, because it is now in the middle
Everything older than D
Nothing, because the old tip C is still reachable from D
items.explanation: When the new tip contains the old one, force makes no difference compared with a normal push.

choices: Only D
D, E and F
C and D
Nothing, since A is shared
items.explanation: Lost commits are those reachable from the old tip but not the new one: C is reachable from F, D is not.

items.prompt: What is origin/main on your machine?
choices: Your last-known copy of where the remote's main pointed
The live position of main on the server
A branch only you can push to
items.explanation: It is a remembered position, updated only when you talk to the remote.

items.prompt: What does git fetch do?
choices: Merges the remote's work into your current branch
Downloads the remote's new commits and updates origin/* without touching your branches
Pushes your commits to the remote
items.explanation: Fetch only updates your view of the remote.

items.prompt: A teammate pushes to the remote. When does your origin/main change?
choices: Immediately, as the server notifies you
Only when you restart your editor
Next time you fetch, pull, or push to that remote
items.explanation: Git has no live push notification; your view updates when you contact the remote.

items.prompt: What is a stale view of the remote?
choices: A remembered remote position older than the real one
A branch with no commits
A commit with a missing parent
items.explanation: Stale means the remote has moved since you last looked.

items.prompt: Who loses work in the incident described in this unit?
choices: The developer who force-pushed
The teammate whose commit was dropped from the branch
Nobody; the commits are merged automatically
items.explanation: The force-pusher's own work lands; the other person's is displaced.

items.prompt: What combination actually causes the loss?
choices: Rebasing your own local commits
Having a teammate who pushes often
Force-pushing while your view of a shared branch is out of date
items.explanation: Rebase alone is local and harmless; force plus stale is the hazard.

items.prompt: Is the teammate's commit still on their own machine?
choices: Yes, their clone still holds it
No, a force-push reaches into every clone
Only if they enable a backup setting
items.explanation: A push changes the server's pointer, not other people's clones.

items.prompt: What fixes a stale view?
choices: Rebasing again
Fetching, then reading what arrived
Pushing twice
items.explanation: Only contacting the remote refreshes your picture of it.

items.prompt: Last fetch was 9:00. A teammate pushed at 9:30. You rebase and plain-force-push at 10:00. What happens to the 9:30 commit?
choices: It is merged in automatically
The push is rejected
It is moved to a new branch
It is dropped from the branch
items.explanation: Plain force never compares against the remote, so the 9:30 commit is overwritten.
items.reference:
Three copies of the branch
💻 your local branch
🧠 origin/name: what you last saw
🌐 the real remote: may have moved
Why: only a fetch refreshes the middle one.
items.learnMore:
Your picture of the remote is a snapshot

origin/name records what the remote looked like at your last contact. The real remote keeps moving as teammates push.

Common mistake

Assuming a quiet afternoon means nothing changed. Silence on your machine says nothing about the server.
items.reflection: Think of a shared whiteboard photographed this morning. When would you trust the photo, and when would you walk over and look at the board?

items.prompt: git status says your branch is up to date with origin/feature. Does that prove the remote has no new commits?
choices: No, it only compares your branch with your stored copy of the remote
Yes, status asks the server directly
Yes, but only for the first hour
No, it only checks the working tree files
items.explanation: Status uses the remembered origin/feature, which may be stale.

items.prompt: You fetched at 9:45 and rebased onto what arrived. At 9:50 a teammate pushes again. At 10:00 you run a plain force-push. What is the outcome?
choices: Nothing is lost, since you fetched
The 9:50 commit is lost, even though you fetched recently
Git rejects the push automatically
Only your own commits are replaced
items.explanation: A fetch narrows the gap but never closes it; anything pushed after it is invisible to you.

choices: Any branch with a pull request open
The default branch of the project
One that only you ever push to
A branch with at least two reviewers
items.explanation: If nobody else pushes there, the remote can never hold commits you lack.

items.prompt: A normal push succeeds when:
choices: You have not pushed before
The remote's current tip is an ancestor of the tip you push
The branch name matches exactly
items.explanation: That makes the move a pure addition of commits.

items.prompt: A push rejected with 'fetch first' means:
choices: Your repository is corrupted
Your network connection dropped
The remote has commits your local branch does not contain
items.explanation: The ancestor check failed because the remote knows something you do not.

items.prompt: What is a fast-forward?
choices: Moving a branch pointer forward along a line it already contains
Skipping tests before pushing
Compressing the commit history
items.explanation: The new tip simply sits further along the same chain.

items.prompt: After a rejected push, the right next step is to:
choices: Add --force to the same command
Fetch and integrate what arrived, then push again
Delete the branch and start over
items.explanation: The rejection is information; integrate it.

items.prompt: You are strictly ahead of the remote and push normally. The result?
choices: Rejected
Merged into a new branch
Accepted
items.explanation: The remote's tip is an ancestor of yours.

items.prompt: Who enforces the ancestor check?
choices: The remote server when it receives the push
Your local git before sending
The code reviewer
items.explanation: The server decides whether to move its own pointer.

items.prompt: Which flag disables this protection?
choices: --verbose
--force
--set-upstream
items.explanation: Force asks the server to move the pointer without the ancestor question.

items.prompt: A plain push can never drop commits from the remote branch. True?
choices: False; it overwrites silently
False; it deletes old branches
True; it only adds
items.explanation: The ancestor rule guarantees nothing reachable before becomes unreachable.

items.prompt: You rebase commits that were already pushed, and no teammate pushed anything. A plain push is rejected. Why?
choices: The remote's old tip is not an ancestor of your rewritten tip
Someone else must have pushed meanwhile
The rebase deleted your remote-tracking branch
Plain push refuses all rebased branches by policy
items.explanation: Rebasing gave your commits new hashes, so the old tip is no longer in your history.
items.reference:
Normal push check
✅ remote tip is my ancestor → accepted
⛔ remote has commits I lack → rejected
⚠️ --force skips the question
Why: only additions are allowed unless you explicitly override.
items.learnMore:
The check protects the remote's history

It does not judge your code or your branch. It asks only whether moving the pointer would make existing commits unreachable.

Common mistake

Treating a rejection as a nuisance to bypass. It is a report that the remote knows something you do not.
items.reflection: A shared folder only lets you save a file if your copy includes the latest saved version. Where else do you see a rule like that, and what does it protect?

Rejected, because D is not an ancestor of E
Accepted and D dropped
Accepted only for the first commit
items.explanation: The tips diverge, so the move would lose D.

Accepted but D is rewritten

choices: Yes, force is the intended fix
Delete the remote branch first
Push to a new branch name and ignore it
Fetch, look at what arrived, integrate it, then push normally
items.explanation: The rejection prevented a loss; forcing would cause the very loss it flagged.

items.prompt: What does --force-with-lease check before overwriting?
choices: That your code compiles
That nobody is online
That the remote still points where you last saw it
items.explanation: It compares the live remote tip with your stored origin/name.

items.prompt: The remote moved since your last fetch. A lease push does what?
choices: Refuses and tells you why
Overwrites it anyway
Merges the new commit silently
items.explanation: The expected position no longer matches, so the push is rejected.

items.prompt: Can a lease push still rewrite history?
choices: No, it only adds commits
Yes, when the remote has not moved
Only on the default branch
items.explanation: It is force with a guard, not a ban on rewriting.

items.prompt: How does plain --force differ from the lease?
choices: Force is slower
The lease only works with tags
Force does not check the remote; the lease does
items.explanation: The lease adds one safety comparison.

items.prompt: After a lease rejection you should:
choices: Fetch, inspect what arrived, and reconcile
Re-run with --force
Delete origin/name
items.explanation: Refresh your view before deciding anything.

items.prompt: Which stored value does the lease compare against by default?
choices: Your working directory
Your remote-tracking branch, like origin/feature
The last commit message
items.explanation: That is the last position you recorded for the remote.

items.prompt: Is the lease a replacement for reading what changed on the remote?
choices: Yes, it reads everything for you
Yes, but only on shared branches
No, it is a safety net on top of that habit
items.explanation: It checks whether the remote moved, not whether you understand the change.

items.prompt: Why prefer the lease for a rewritten feature branch?
choices: It allows the rewrite while catching surprise commits
It makes commits smaller
It avoids the need to fetch ever
items.explanation: It balances the need to force with protection from unseen work.

items.prompt: Remote tip is D, but your origin/feature says C. You run a lease push of your rewrite E. Outcome?
choices: Accepted, E replaces D
Accepted, E merged with D
Rejected, because the remote is D, not C
Rejected only if D was authored by someone else
items.explanation: The remote does not match what you last saw, so the lease fails.
items.reference:
Force vs lease
🔓 force: no questions asked
🔒 lease: has the remote moved since I looked?
🔄 rejected → fetch, inspect, reconcile
Why: it keeps rewrites possible while refusing to overwrite unseen work.
items.learnMore:
A lease is a conditional overwrite

You tell git the position you expect. If the remote disagrees, nothing is written.

Common mistake

Thinking the lease makes force-pushing free of risk. It checks one condition only.
items.reflection: Think of editing a shared spreadsheet row only if the version number is still the one you loaded. What is the parallel, and what can still go wrong?

Accepted; E replaces the remote's position

The lease checks the code, the ancestor check checks the message

There is no difference

choices: The lease can only be used once per day
Nothing changed, so it will fail again until you fetch and reconcile
It will succeed but corrupt history
The server locks the branch for an hour
items.explanation: Your expected value is unchanged; you must refresh and integrate first.

items.prompt: Rebasing a commit gives it:
choices: The same hash with a new date
A new hash
No hash until pushed
items.explanation: The hash covers the parent, so replaying creates new commits.

items.prompt: A git commit hash is:
choices: A random number assigned by the server
The commit's line count
A 40-character SHA-1 identifier computed from the commit's content and parent
items.explanation: Change the content, message or parent and the hash changes.

items.prompt: What happens to commits after a rewritten one?
choices: They get new hashes too
They keep their old ones
They are deleted
items.explanation: Each includes its parent's hash.

items.prompt: A teammate who built on your old commits sees what after your force-push?
choices: Their branch updates itself
Their branch still points at the old chain
Their work disappears
items.explanation: Their clone is independent until they fetch and act.

items.prompt: A teammate then runs git pull. A common outcome is:
choices: A clean fast-forward
Their local commits are deleted
Old and new copies of the same changes appear together
items.explanation: The merge joins two parallel versions of the same work.

items.prompt: Which rewrite is generally safe?
choices: Commits nobody else has fetched yet
Any commit older than a week
Any commit on main
items.explanation: No one depends on commits no one has.

items.prompt: Is amending only the message of a pushed commit a rewrite?
choices: No, messages are metadata only
Yes; the message is part of the hash
Only if you change files too
items.explanation: A new hash means a new commit.

items.prompt: Which is a sensible team rule for shared branches?
choices: Always squash after pushing
Rewrite whenever history looks messy
Add new commits; avoid rewriting what others may have
items.explanation: Rewrites on shared branches impose work on everyone else.

items.prompt: You amend only a commit message and force-push. Whose history is affected?
choices: Only yours
Only the commit's author
Everyone who has the old commit or any commit built on it
Nobody, since the files are unchanged
items.explanation: New hashes down the chain make a parallel history for all holders.
items.reference:
Why rewriting spreads
🔢 hash covers content + parent
⛓️ change one → all later hashes change
👥 holders of the old chain now diverge
Why: a rewrite is new commits, not an edit in place.
items.learnMore:
A rewrite is a replacement

The old commits still exist for anyone who has them. The rewritten ones are different objects that happen to carry the same changes.

Common mistake

Believing teammates automatically follow the new history. They have to act to move over.
items.reflection: If you edit a document that others already copied, how do you let them know, and how do they merge your new version with their edits?

The remote still matched your tracking ref
items.explanation: It is a statement about the tracking ref.

items.prompt: What does --force-if-includes add?
choices: A check that your local branch includes the remote-tracking tip
Faster pushes
Automatic merging
items.explanation: It closes the gap left by silent tracking-ref updates.

items.prompt: Which habit best complements the lease?
choices: Using shorter branch names
Reading git log origin/name before pushing
Pushing late at night
items.explanation: Reviewing what arrived makes the lease meaningful.

items.prompt: Spelling out --force-with-lease=name:hash does what?
choices: Disables the lease
Pushes tags too
Fixes the expected remote tip to a value you chose
items.explanation: The lease no longer follows whatever the tracking ref holds.

items.prompt: Does a lease on branch feature protect branch release?
choices: No, it concerns the ref being pushed
Yes, all branches
Yes, but only with --all
items.explanation: Each ref is checked independently.

items.prompt: The lease replaces having a team convention for shared branches. True?
choices: True
False; it is one layer among several
True, for main only
items.explanation: Conventions about who rewrites what still matter.

items.prompt: A background fetch brought D into origin/feature at 10:00. At 10:05 you rebase your own commits, never having looked at D, and run a lease push. Result?
choices: The push is rejected
D is merged automatically
Only your newest commit is pushed
The push succeeds and D is dropped
items.explanation: The remote matches origin/feature (D), so the lease is satisfied despite your branch lacking D.
items.reference:
Where the lease can mislead
🤖 auto-fetch updates origin/name
📍 lease passes: remote == origin/name
❓ did my branch include that work?
Why: the lease checks the tracking ref, not your understanding.
items.learnMore:
A check is only as good as its reference

The lease trusts origin/name as proof that you looked. Tools that update it silently weaken that proof.

Common mistake

Treating a successful push as proof your branch had everything. It proved only that the remote matched your record.
items.reflection: Think of a door that opens only if the number on your ticket matches the board. What if someone else updates your ticket for you?

items.prompt: Which guard turns that situation into a rejection?

items.prompt: Who most likely still has a displaced commit?
choices: The person who created and pushed it
The person who force-pushed
Every clone automatically
items.explanation: Their clone made it and kept it.

items.prompt: What does git reflog show?
choices: The remote server's history
Where your local refs and HEAD used to point
Every commit ever made by anyone
items.explanation: It is a local log of ref movements.

items.prompt: Can your reflog contain a commit you never fetched?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, from the server
No
items.explanation: It only records places your own refs have been.

items.prompt: What identifies a commit uniquely?
choices: Its 40-character hash
Its message
Its author's name
items.explanation: The hash is derived from the commit's content and parent.

items.prompt: A good first step after discovering a loss is to:
choices: Force-push again to fix it
Tell the team and stop pushing to that branch
Delete the branch
items.explanation: Further pushes can cause more overwrites.

items.prompt: How can a commit be restored once you have its hash?
choices: Re-run git init
Reinstall git
Create a branch there or cherry-pick it
items.explanation: Either gives it a reference again.

items.prompt: What eventually removes unreferenced commits from a repository?
choices: Garbage collection
The next fetch
The next commit
items.explanation: Unreachable objects are pruned after a grace period.

items.prompt: Why should the team agree on branch state before pushing again?
choices: To save disk space
To avoid overwriting the restored work
To shorten hashes
items.explanation: A second uncoordinated push repeats the problem.

items.prompt: Where is the displaced commit D most reliably available?
choices: The force-pusher's reflog
The teammate's clone that created it
A fresh clone of the repo
The remote branch's visible log
items.explanation: The force-pusher never had D and a fresh clone only sees the branch.
items.reference:
Who holds what
👤 teammate clone: has D
💻 pusher clone: never had D
🌐 server: maybe, until garbage collection
Why: recovery starts with finding the hash and the clone that has the object.
items.learnMore:
Unreachable is not yet erased

Until garbage collection removes it, an object can be restored if you have its hash and a repository that stores it.

Common mistake

Searching the wrong clone. A reflog only knows about commits that clone has seen.
items.reflection: If your shared drive deleted a file you had never opened, who might still have a copy, and how would you ask for it?
